procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of confirmation and continuation of detention made on May 5, 1971, under sec. 12 of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, following the petitioner's detention on February 5, 1971, under s. 3 of the same Act.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The case originated as a Writ Petition (No. 287 of 1971) under Article 32 of the Constitution of India directly in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court dismissed the writ petition, upholding the detention order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the confirmation of the detention order was made one day after the expiration of the period of 3 months from the date of detention.

facts: The petitioner was detained on February 5, 1971.
The law required the detention order to be confirmed within a period of three months from the date of detention.
The State Government confirmed the detention order on May 5, 1971.
The petitioner argued that the three-month period expired on the midnight of May 4, 1971, making the confirmation on May 5 invalid as it was one day late.
law: The Court established a general rule for computing a period of time that runs 'from' a specific day or event.
Citing English legal precedent (Halsbury's Laws of England and various cases), the rule is to exclude the first day (the day of the event) and include the last day of the period.
application: To calculate the three-month period, the Court applied the established legal rule.
The period was 'from the date of detention', which was February 5, 1971.
Following the rule, the Court excluded the date of the detention (February 5, 1971) from the computation.
By excluding the first day, the calculation showed that the three-month period had not yet expired when the confirmation order was made on May 5, 1971.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the order of confirmation was made before the expiration of the three-month period. Therefore, the Court rejected the petitioner's contention that the confirmation was made one day too late.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the confirmation of the detention order was made one day after the expiration of the period of 3 months from the date of detention.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner was detained on February 5, 1971, and the order of confirmation was made on May 5, 1971.
The period of three months from the date of detention expired on the midnight of May 4, 1971.
Therefore, the confirmation and continuation of the detention made on May 5, 1971, was one day late and not valid.
respondent_arguments: The confirmation of the detention order on May 5, 1971, was made within the statutory three-month period and was therefore valid.

statutes.act_name: The Act (name not specified in text)

cases.principle: When computing a period 'within twenty-one days after their execution', the day of execution is to be excluded.

cases.case_name: Goldsmiths' Company v. The West Metropolitan Railway Company
cases.principle: Where a particular time is given from a certain date within which an act is to be done, the day of that date is to be excluded.
The expression 'fifteen days from the date of commencement of the Policy' was construed as excluding the first date.

cases.case_name: Marren v. Dawson Bentley & Co. Ltd.
cases.principle: For purposes of computing the period of limitation, the date of the accident (being the date of the cause of action) was excluded.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When computing a prescribed period of time 'from' a certain date within which an act is to be done, the day of that date is to be excluded from the calculation.
obiter: Courts have drawn a distinction between a term created within which an act may be done and a time limited for the doing of an act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that there is a distinction between a term created within which an act may be done and a time limited for the doing of an act. The well-established rule is that where a particular time is given from a certain date within which an act is to be done, the day of that date is to be excluded from the calculation. Therefore, the effect of defining a period from one day until another is to exclude the first day and include the last day, meaning the confirmation order was made before the expiration of the three-month period.
legal_tests_applied: The rule that where a particular time is given from a certain date within which an act is to be done, the day on that date is to be excluded.
The distinction between a term created within which an act may be done and a time limited for the doing of an act.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner's calculation of the three-month period was incorrect because it failed to apply the established legal rule of excluding the first day (the date of detention) when computing the time period.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because, by correctly applying the legal rule to exclude the first day of detention from the calculation, the order of confirmation made on May 5, 1971, fell within the statutory three-month period.
